At a glance

Best months
  • September to November across the south and the east, when the passerines are singing and the mallee and the box-ironbark are in flower
  • May to October is the window in the tropical north, when the wet has drained and the roads reopen
Regions
The Top End: Darwin, Kakadu and the Adelaide RiverBroome and Roebuck BayThe north Kimberley: Kununurra, the Ord and the Mitchell PlateauThe Wet Tropics: Cairns, the Atherton Tableland and the tropical coastCape York: Kutini-Payamu, Rinyirru and WeipaThe Queensland inland: the Gulf savannah and CloncurrySoutheast Queensland and the border rangesThe Sydney basin and the sandstone countryThe Hunter and the BarringtonsThe Illawarra and the Shoalhaven: Barren Grounds to Jervis BayThe Riverina and the central westThe far west and the corner country: Broken Hill to BirdsvilleCanberra and the high countryMelbourne and Port Phillip: Werribee and the You YangsThe Victorian coast: Port Fairy, Phillip Island and Wilsons PromontoryThe Victorian Mallee and the box-ironbarkFar East Gippsland and the Croajingolong coastSouth Australia: Gluepot, the Flinders and the arid northThe southern coast: Yorke Peninsula, Kangaroo Island and Bool LagoonSouthwest Western Australia: Cheynes Beach and the StirlingsPerth, Rottnest and the mid-west coastTasmania and Bass StraitThe Red CentreLord Howe and Norfolk: the Tasman islandsChristmas Island and the Indian Ocean territories
Routes
The Top End and the Red Centre13 daysBroome and the north Kimberley14 daysTropical Queensland: the Wet Tropics, Cape York and the savannah22 daysBrisbane, the border ranges and the Tasman islands14 daysThe southeast coast, Sydney to Melbourne20 daysTasmania and Bass Strait9 daysThe Mallee, the Riverina and the corner country17 daysSouth Australia: Gluepot, the Flinders and the southern coast12 daysThe southwest, Perth and Christmas Island17 days
Getting in
Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Darwin all take long-haul flights, and the domestic network reaches every regional base in this guide.
Getting around
A hire car is the only practical way to bird most of these regions, and the distances between them are continental. Internal flights save days on the Top End, Cape York and the west.

13 days

The Top End and the Red Centre

Darwin (DRW), Darwin 3 nights, Fogg Dam and the Adelaide River 1 night, Kakadu 3 nights, the flight south to Alice Springs, Alice Springs 4 nights, Alice Springs (ASP) out

The tropical north works best late in the dry season, when the floodplain birds crowd the last water. Darwin holds the mangrove and monsoon forest species within half an hour of the airport, and Kakadu earns three nights for the sandstone country above the wetlands. The flight south to Alice Springs takes two hours and opens the desert, where the ranges hold the grasswrens and the town water carries the finches.

  1. Broome (BME)in
  2. 1Roebuck Bay, Broome
  3. 2Broome Bird Observatory
  4. 3Kununurra
  5. 4Lake Argyle
  6. 5Parrys Lagoon Nature Reserve
  7. 6Mitchell Plateau
  8. Darwin (DRW)out

14 days

Broome and the north Kimberley

Broome (BME), Broome 4 nights, the drive east to Kununurra 2 nights, Kununurra and Lake Argyle 3 nights, the Mitchell Plateau 3 nights, the drive to Darwin 1 night, Darwin (DRW) out

Roebuck Bay carries the biggest wader flocks in the country, and the birds are in breeding plumage from late March. The road east crosses savannah and ends at the Ord, where the lagoons and the sandstone gorges hold a different set again. The Mitchell Plateau needs a high clearance four wheel drive, spare fuel and a day in hand for the track.

  1. Cairns (CNS)in

  3. 2Daintree River

  14. Townsville (TSV)out

22 days

Tropical Queensland: the Wet Tropics, Cape York and the savannah

Cairns (CNS), Cairns and the Daintree 4 nights, Julatten and the Atherton Tableland 4 nights, Rinyirru 3 nights, the flight to Lockhart River 4 nights, Weipa 2 nights, the savannah road to Georgetown and Cloncurry 3 nights, Townsville 1 night, Townsville (TSV) out

Three weeks covers the wet forest, the peninsula and the dry savannah behind them. The Wet Tropics deliver the rainforest endemics from sea level to the tableland, and eight nights there is a working minimum. Kutini-Payamu is reached by air through Lockhart River and holds the birds shared with the tropics to the north, and the savannah road out to Cloncurry adds the finches and the spinifex birds on the way to the coast.

  1. Brisbane (BNE)in
  2. 1Lamington National Park
  3. 2Springbrook National Park
  4. 3Lord Howe Island
  5. 4Norfolk Island

14 days

Brisbane, the border ranges and the Tasman islands

Brisbane (BNE), Lamington 3 nights, Springbrook 2 nights, the flight to Lord Howe Island 4 nights, Norfolk Island 4 nights, Brisbane (BNE) out

The subtropical rainforest on the border ranges sits ninety minutes from Brisbane and holds Albert's Lyrebird, the whipbirds and three bowerbirds. Both islands are reached by air from the east coast and each carries birds that breed only there. Lord Howe wants four nights for the woodhen and the petrel colony on the mountain, and Norfolk wants the same for its forest birds.

20 days

The southeast coast, Sydney to Melbourne

Sydney (SYD), Sydney 2 nights, the Capertee Valley 2 nights, Barrington Tops 2 nights, the Hunter estuary 2 nights, Barren Grounds and Jervis Bay 3 nights, Canberra 2 nights, Green Cape and Mallacoota 3 nights, Wilsons Promontory and Phillip Island 2 nights, Werribee 1 night, Melbourne (MEL) out

One drive links the sandstone, the estuaries, the high country and the southern heath. The Capertee Valley is the Regent Honeyeater's stronghold and lies three hours inland from Sydney, the Hunter takes the summer waders, and Barren Grounds holds both bristlebirds. Canberra adds the alpine edge at Namadgi, and the coast past Green Cape runs into the East Gippsland forests. The Western Treatment Plant at Werribee finishes the route within an hour of the airport and needs a permit for vehicle access.

9 days

Tasmania and Bass Strait

Hobart (HBA), Bruny Island 3 nights, Mount Field 1 night, Eaglehawk Neck 2 nights, Melaleuca by light aircraft, Hobart 2 nights, Hobart (HBA) out

Every Tasmanian endemic lives within two hours of Hobart, and Bruny Island holds all twelve on a single small island. The pelagic out of Eaglehawk Neck reaches shelf water in about ninety minutes and brings the albatrosses close. The light aircraft flight to Melaleuca is the dependable way to see Orange-bellied Parrots at the breeding ground, and it wants a spare day for weather.

17 days

The Mallee, the Riverina and the corner country

Melbourne (MEL), Chiltern 2 nights, the Riverina 3 nights, Round Hill 1 night, Hattah and Wyperfeld 3 nights, Broken Hill 2 nights, Sturt National Park 2 nights, Innamincka and the Birdsville Track 3 nights, Adelaide (ADL) out

The route runs from the box-ironbark woodland into the mallee and then into the stony desert, and the birds change with the rainfall at every step. Chiltern and Round Hill carry the woodland honeyeaters, Hattah and Wyperfeld hold the Mallee Emu-wren and the whipbird, and the corner country beyond Broken Hill is where the grasswrens and the desert chats live. The Strzelecki and Birdsville Tracks are unsealed, so this leg needs a high clearance vehicle, water and spare fuel.

12 days

South Australia: Gluepot, the Flinders and the southern coast

Adelaide (ADL), Gluepot 3 nights, Port Augusta 1 night, the Flinders Ranges 3 nights, Innes 1 night, Kangaroo Island 2 nights, Bool Lagoon 1 night, Adelaide (ADL) out

Gluepot is mallee reserve three hours northeast of the city and holds the Black-eared Miner, the Red-lored Whistler and the Striated Grasswren. The Flinders Ranges add the Short-tailed Grasswren and the arid woodland birds, with the saltbush around Port Augusta on the way. The southern half of the loop is coastal, where Innes takes the Western Whipbird, Kangaroo Island carries its own races and Bool Lagoon fills with waterbirds in a wet year. The island ferry takes vehicles and wants booking ahead.

17 days

The southwest, Perth and Christmas Island

Perth (PER), Perth and Rottnest 2 nights, the Stirling Range 2 nights, Cheynes Beach 4 nights, Fitzgerald River 1 night, Kalbarri 2 nights, the flight to Christmas Island 5 nights, Perth (PER) out

The southwest corner holds a set of endemics found in no other state, and Cheynes Beach puts the Noisy Scrub-bird, the Western Bristlebird and the Western Whipbird within one small area of heath. Rottnest covers the seabirds and the terns, and Kalbarri adds the gorge and heath birds north of the city. Christmas Island is a four hour flight from Perth and holds a frigatebird, a hawk-owl and a goshawk that breed only there, so five nights makes it worth the crossing.

The Top End: Darwin, Kakadu and the Adelaide River

Arnhem Land escarpment endemics above monsoon floodplains

Darwin sits within a short drive of monsoon forest, mangrove creeks and vast floodplains, and the Arnhem Land escarpment rises behind Kakadu. Four bird species live in the Top End and nowhere else. Fogg Dam alone has recorded more than 230 species.

  • Habitat: Habitats run from tidal mudflats and mangrove creeks through monsoon forest and tropical woodland to floodplains that hold water for several months of the year, and then up onto the sandstone escarpment and plateau of Arnhem Land.
  • When: The dry season from May to October brings mild weather and falling water levels, which concentrates waterbirds and seed eaters on the shrinking wetlands. The wet season from December to April is hot and humid, water is widely dispersed and heavy rain can close tracks.
  • Getting there: Darwin takes daily flights from every mainland capital and has regular international services from Southeast Asia. Sealed highways run east to Kakadu, south to Katherine and west towards the Kimberley, and a 2WD car reaches most sites. Remote corners of Kakadu such as Jim Jim and Twin Falls need a 4WD.
  • Look for: Rainbow Pitta, White-throated Grasswren, Chestnut-quilled Rock Pigeon, White-lined Honeyeater, Black-banded Fruit Dove, Chestnut Rail, Rufous Owl, Partridge Pigeon, Hooded Parrot, Sandstone Shrikethrush, Great-billed Heron, Little Kingfisher
  • Stops:
    • : A reserve built to water a rice scheme and now holding huge concentrations of waterbirds, with over 230 species recorded. Magpie Goose, Comb-crested Jacana and White-browed Crake are the regulars, and Rainbow Pitta and Little Kingfisher use the fringing forest.
    • : Mangrove and coastal monsoon forest at the northern end of Casuarina Coastal Reserve. Chestnut Rail works the creek mud, Rainbow Pitta and Arafura Fantail hold the forest, and the nearby Lee Point shore-point is a high tide roost for shorebirds.
    • : A small swamp and grassland south-east of Darwin that you enter on foot. Magpie Goose and Pied Heron roost here, Radjah Shelduck and Black-necked Stork feed on the water, and King Quail and Tawny Grassbird live in the surrounding grass.
    • : The park pairs the Yellow Water billabongs on the South Alligator floodplain with the Arnhem Land sandstone escarpment. Waterbirds, Great-billed Heron and Red Goshawk belong to the wetlands, while Partridge Pigeon, White-lined Honeyeater, Black-banded Fruit Dove and Sandstone Shrikethrush belong to the rock country.
    • : The point where the Arnhem Highway crosses the river on the drive between Darwin and Kakadu. Mangroves along the bank hold Mangrove Golden Whistler and Arafura Fantail, and the river itself carries Magpie Goose, Radjah Shelduck and Black-necked Stork.
    • : Forty-two hectares of gardens with a rainforest section, a short walk from the city centre. They have long been one of Australia's most reliable places for Rufous Owl, Barking Owl roosts in the larger trees, and Orange-footed Scrubfowl are common and tame.
  • Also covers: Adelaide River Crossing, Buffalo Creek, Darwin Botanic Gardens, Fogg Dam, Kakadu National Park, Knuckeys Lagoon, Top End
  • Also watch for: Saltwater Crocodiles are regular along the Adelaide River and through the mangrove creeks near Darwin, and Black Wallaroo and Short-eared Rock Wallaby live on the Kakadu escarpment.

Broome and Roebuck Bay

the great shorebird bay of tropical Australia

Roebuck Bay is one of the most significant shorebird sites in Australia, visited by some 120,000 birds a year. A bird observatory established in 1988 overlooks the bay from the east. Mangrove creeks and open plains sit within a short drive of the town.

  • Habitat: Vast intertidal mudflats meet mangrove fringes, red pindan soils and the grassy termite mound plains that run inland from the bay.
  • When: September to April is the peak for shorebirds, though juveniles and immatures of many species overwinter and can be found year round. Aim for high tide, when the rising water pushes birds off the flats onto roosts along the shoreline.
  • Getting there: Broome has an international airport and scheduled flights from Perth. The observatory road east of town is unsealed and can close during the wet season, so check road conditions before setting out.
  • Look for: Asian Dowitcher, Common Redshank, Broad-billed Sandpiper, Great Knot, Bar-tailed Godwit, Yellow Chat, White-breasted Whistler, Mangrove Golden Whistler, Dusky Gerygone, Oriental Pratincole, Grey-tailed Tattler, Far Eastern Curlew
  • Stops:
    • : Tidal mudflats that around 120,000 shorebirds use each year. Asian Dowitcher, Broad-billed Sandpiper, Great Knot and Bar-tailed Godwit are among them, and because many young birds stay through the southern winter the bay repays a visit at any season.
    • : The observatory was established in 1988 on the shore of Roebuck Bay and looks out over the roosts. Beyond the shorebirds, the surrounding mangrove and pindan hold White-breasted Whistler, Mangrove Golden Whistler and Yellow Chat.
  • Also covers: Broome Bird Observatory, Roebuck Bay, Broome
  • Also watch for: Agile Wallaby comes in to drink at the bird bath at Broome Bird Observatory, alongside the finches and the flycatchers.

The north Kimberley: Kununurra, the Ord and the Mitchell Plateau

two Kimberley endemics at the end of a hard track

The Mitchell Plateau holds Black Grasswren and Kimberley Honeyeater, two birds found nowhere else. Black Grasswren is reckoned among the hardest Australian birds to see, and its nest and eggs were described only in 1998. Around Kununurra the Ord River, Lake Argyle and the Parry Lagoons wetlands gather finches, chats and waterbirds.

  • Habitat: Sandstone escarpments and deep gorges cut the plateau, with pandanus lined creeks and waterfalls below. Around Kununurra a large dammed lake, riverine forest and floodplain wetlands sit within savannah woodland.
  • When: Travel through the Kimberley is realistic from about May to the end of October. The wet season brings road closures and the risk of cyclones, so watch the forecasts before committing to a route.
  • Getting there: Kununurra takes scheduled flights from Perth. The Gibb River Road crosses the heart of the Kimberley and closes for long stretches of the wet season. Reaching the Mitchell Plateau means several hundred kilometres of unsealed road and then a rough final track, and a 4WD is essential.
  • Look for: Black Grasswren, Kimberley Honeyeater, White-quilled Rock Pigeon, Purple-crowned Fairywren, Yellow Chat, Gouldian Finch, Yellow-rumped Mannikin, Spinifex Pigeon, Partridge Pigeon, Buff-sided Robin, Sandstone Shrikethrush, Varied Lorikeet
  • Stops:
    • : A town on the Ord River in the East Kimberley and one of Australia's best places for a run of finches. The irrigated farmland of the Weaber Plains to the north holds Yellow-rumped Mannikin and Pictorella Mannikin, and Lily Creek Lagoon on the edge of town carries White-browed Crake and Comb-crested Jacana.
    • : Australia's largest artificial lake, formed when the Ord River was dammed in 1971. Waterbirds and shorebirds gather on it, and the surrounding rock and grassland hold Yellow Chat, Purple-crowned Fairywren, White-quilled Rock Pigeon and Gouldian Finch.
    • : Wetlands on the Ord River floodplain south of Wyndham, with grassland and sandstone country around them. The largest lagoon has a boardwalk and a hide, and as the lagoons shrink through the dry season the waterbirds concentrate on what water is left.
    • : Escarpment, deep gorges and pandanus creek lines in Mitchell River National Park, in the far north of the Kimberley. It is the home of two Kimberley endemics, Black Grasswren and Kimberley Honeyeater, and the remoteness is why the grasswren is rated one of the hardest birds in Australia to see.
  • Also covers: Kununurra, Lake Argyle, Mitchell Plateau, Parrys Lagoon Nature Reserve
  • Also watch for: Freshwater Crocodile lives in the gorge pools of the plateau country, and Common Wallaroo works the sandstone escarpment above them.

The Wet Tropics: Cairns, the Atherton Tableland and the tropical coast

thirteen rainforest endemics within a day of Cairns

Thirteen bird species are restricted to the Cairns and Wet Tropics region, most of them in the upland rainforest of the Atherton Tableland. More than half of Australia's birds occur somewhere in north Queensland, and a week spent between the coast, the tableland and the Daintree can produce over 200 species. Cairns Esplanade puts shorebirds within walking distance of the city.

  • Habitat: Upland rainforest covers the tableland and its crater lakes, lowland rainforest reaches the sea at Mission Beach, and mangroves, tidal flats and freshwater swamps line the coast from Cairns south to Townsville.
  • When: The winter months from May to November are mild with low rainfall. The wet season peaks between December and April, with the heaviest rain in March. Buff-breasted Paradise Kingfisher is present only from October to March.
  • Getting there: Cairns has an international airport, and sealed roads climb to the tableland and run north to the Daintree. Nearly every site works as a day trip by ordinary car from Cairns, the tableland or the Daintree. Accommodation is plentiful across the region.
  • Look for: Southern Cassowary, Victoria's Riflebird, Golden Bowerbird, Tooth-billed Bowerbird, Chowchilla, Fernwren, Atherton Scrubwren, Mountain Thornbill, Bower's Shrikethrush, Grey-headed Robin, Bridled Honeyeater, Macleay's Honeyeater, Pied Monarch, Buff-breasted Paradise Kingfisher, Sarus Crane, Blue-faced Parrotfinch
  • Stops:
    • : Mudflats along the city foreshore that are internationally important for resident and migratory shorebirds. Beach Stone-curlew and Broad-billed Sandpiper are the prizes, and Varied Honeyeater works the trees behind the tide line.
    • : Five hectares of rainforest at Julatten with tracks through the grounds. It is named for the Buff-breasted Paradise Kingfisher that come in to breed over the wet season, and the same tracks find Red-necked Crake, Noisy Pitta and Papuan Frogmouth.
    • : The river and the rainforest around Daintree Village. Dawn boat trips work the quieter arms of the system for Great-billed Heron, Little Kingfisher and Papuan Frogmouth.
    • : Twelve linked lagoons, creeks and channels set in savanna woodland. The water draws Sarus Crane, Black-necked Stork and Comb-crested Jacana, and the woodland around it holds Squatter Pigeon and other dry country birds.
    • : A small swamp with a boardwalk running from the car park to a bird hide, in open woodland south of Julatten. White-browed Crake works the water, and the paperbarks around the car park pull in honeyeaters when they flower, along with Northern Fantail and Blue-faced Parrotfinch.
    • : A seasonal wetland of 57 hectares south of Atherton with over 220 species recorded. It becomes the refuge for waterbirds in the late dry season once the other tableland wetlands go, and Sarus Crane, Brolga and Cotton Pygmy Goose use it.
    • : A strip of lowland rainforest between the ocean and the hills behind. The rainforest here is the most accessible place on the coast for Southern Cassowary, and Pale-vented Bush-hen lives in the same country.
    • : Three thousand hectares of wetland just north of Townsville. Water lies here from the break of the wet until about June, and as the levels drop the waterfowl crowd into what remains, with Brolga, Black-necked Stork, Cotton Pygmy Goose and Little Kingfisher.
  • Also covers: Abattoir Swamp, Atherton Tableland, Cairns Esplanade, Daintree River, Hasties Swamp National Park, Kingfisher Park, Julatten, Mareeba Tropical Savanna and Wetland Reserve, Mission Beach, Townsville Town Common Conservation Park
  • Also watch for: Lumholtz's Tree-Kangaroo, Striped Possum and Musky Rat-kangaroo live in the tableland rainforest, Platypus turn up in the creeks, and Boyd's Forest Dragon is one of the reptiles most often seen by day.

Cape York: Kutini-Payamu, Rinyirru and Weipa

New Guinea birds at their only Australian address

Kutini-Payamu protects Australia's largest area of lowland rainforest and a suite of birds shared with New Guinea. Two species, Golden-shouldered Parrot and White-streaked Honeyeater, occur only on Cape York. Over 320 species have been recorded across the peninsula.

  • Habitat: Lowland rainforest at Iron Range gives way to tropical savannah and grassland studded with termite mounds, with wide saline mangrove deltas and freshwater lagoon systems at Rinyirru and along the western coast near Weipa.
  • When: The dry season runs from May to November, with September the driest month, and late September to early November is the pick of the year. The wet season runs December to April and brings the highest rain in March. Black-winged Monarch and Papuan Pitta are wet season visitors that arrive from October and December and leave by April, so a wet season trip is the only way to see them.
  • Getting there: A 4WD is essential across the Cape, and many roads close through the wet season. Scheduled flights serve Coen, Weipa, Lockhart River, Bamaga and Horn Island, and local 4WD hire is available in most of those towns. Stops are far apart, so obtain supplies before setting off. Seeing most of the Cape specialities takes at least nine days.
  • Look for: Palm Cockatoo, Papuan Eclectus, Red-cheeked Parrot, Yellow-billed Kingfisher, Golden-shouldered Parrot, White-streaked Honeyeater, Northern Scrub Robin, Magnificent Riflebird, Trumpet Manucode, Fawn-breasted Bowerbird, Frill-necked Monarch, Black-winged Monarch, Papuan Pitta, Tropical Scrubwren, Black-backed Butcherbird, Green-backed Honeyeater
  • Stops:
    • : Kutini-Payamu protects the largest area of lowland rainforest in Australia and carries the longest list of key species of any site in the standard guide. Palm Cockatoo, Magnificent Riflebird and Northern Scrub Robin are here, and the airstrip at Lockhart River is the way in when the wet season closes the road.
    • : The largest national park on Cape York runs from coastal estuaries and mangroves through wetlands and grassland to sandstone hills in the south. Star Finch, Crimson Finch, Sarus Crane and Eastern Grass Owl are the birds to look for.
    • : Weipa is the largest town on the peninsula and sits among vine forest, wetland, mangrove and coastal dune. It holds the only known mainland roost of Lesser Frigatebird and Great Frigatebird, which fly in over the town in the evening, and Spotted Whistling Duck is on the local wetlands.
  • Also covers: Lockhart River, for Kutini-Payamu (Iron Range), Rinyirru (Lakefield) National Park, Weipa
  • Also watch for: Spotted Cuscus, Common Cuscus, Striped Possum and Cape York Melomys live in the Iron Range rainforest, and Spectacled Flying-Fox feed in coastal town gardens after dark.

The Queensland inland: the Gulf savannah and Cloncurry

eight finch species coming to water at one outback dam

Cumberland Dam, an old mine site west of Georgetown, has recorded eight species of finch coming in to drink. This is the Gulf of Carpentaria savannah, and further inland the spinifex hills around Cloncurry and Mount Isa hold Kalkadoon Grasswren and Carpentarian Grasswren. Distances between sites here are enormous.

  • Habitat: Open grassy woodland scattered with termite mounds surrounds the dams of the Gulf savannah. Around Cloncurry and Mount Isa the country turns to spinifex clad stony hills cut by creek gullies.
  • When: Autumn and spring bring mild days and nights and are the best times to travel. Late in the dry season is the moment for finches, when surface water grows scarce and birds come to the dams to drink early in the morning. Summer averages around 37 degrees in the north and can climb into the mid forties in the southwest.
  • Getting there: Sealed development roads link Cairns to Georgetown and run on towards the Gulf, and a 2WD car reaches the main sites. Legs between towns are long, so plan fuel and water for each one. Camping and town accommodation are both available.
  • Look for: Gouldian Finch, Masked Finch, Black-throated Finch, Pictorella Mannikin, Squatter Pigeon, Kalkadoon Grasswren, Carpentarian Grasswren, Spinifex Pigeon, Painted Finch, Australian Ringneck, Spinifexbird, Grey Falcon, Rufous-throated Honeyeater, Yellow-tinted Honeyeater
  • Stops:
    • : An old mine site holds a pair of dams, and grassy woodland and termite mounds surround them. Eight species of finch have been recorded here, and the birding sharpens towards the end of the dry season when surface water elsewhere runs out.
    • : Dams in open country north of Cloncurry. Caspian Tern and Great Crested Grebe turn up here in flocks, which is unusual for both, and Spotted Bowerbird and the local pale race of Australian Ringneck are around the town.
  • Also covers: Clem Walton Park, Cloncurry, Cumberland Dam, Georgetown
  • Also watch for: Purple-necked Rock-Wallaby frequents the cliff bases known as Blackrock at Lake Moondarra north of Mount Isa, on the same track the finches use to drink.

Southeast Queensland and the border ranges

Albert's Lyrebird in Gondwanan rainforest on the Scenic Rim

The border ranges south of Brisbane are called the Scenic Rim, and they hold one of the largest upland subtropical rainforest remnants in the world along with Australia's most northerly cool temperate rainforest of Antarctic Beech. Lamington is the classic site, with Albert's Lyrebird and Rufous Scrubbird among its birds. Bowerbirds around the Green Mountains precinct are hand tame.

  • Habitat: Upland subtropical rainforest covers the ranges, with stands of Antarctic Beech on the highest ridges and drier eucalypt forest and woodland on the slopes below. Coastal heathland, mudflats and mangroves lie out towards the sea.
  • When: Autumn brings mild days across the southeast and is a comfortable time to walk the rainforest tracks. Coastal accommodation fills through the summer school holidays from mid December to late January, so book well ahead if travelling then.
  • Getting there: Lamington divides into two sections, Green Mountains and Binna Burra, each reached by a sealed road climbing from the Pacific Highway south of Brisbane. Ordinary cars manage both. Each section has lodge and national park camping nearby, and bush camping in the remote parts is limited to walkers and open only between February and November.
  • Look for: Albert's Lyrebird, Rufous Scrubbird, Paradise Riflebird, Regent Bowerbird, Australian Logrunner, Noisy Pitta, Russet-tailed Thrush, Marbled Frogmouth, Green Catbird, Pale-vented Bush-hen, Sooty Owl, Satin Bowerbird
  • Stops:
    • : Twenty thousand hectares of subtropical rainforest and the most northerly Antarctic Beech forest in Australia, on the McPherson Range, with 160 kilometres of marked track. Albert's Lyrebird, Rufous Scrubbird, Paradise Riflebird and Australian Logrunner are the birds people come for.
    • : The Green Mountains precinct at the top of the Lamington plateau, and the start of the Border Track and the Box Forest Circuit. Regent Bowerbird, Satin Bowerbird, Australian King Parrot and Crimson Rosella are hand-tame around the buildings.
  • Also covers: Lamington National Park, O'Reilly's Rainforest Retreat, SE Queensland, Springbrook National Park
  • Also watch for: Koalas laze in the eucalypts around the campsites in the border ranges, where they are easiest to pick out during the day.

The Sydney basin and the sandstone country

one endemic bound to the Sydney sandstone

Rockwarbler is the only bird endemic to the Sydney region, restricted to sandstone and nearby limestone formations within about 250 kilometres of the city. Royal National Park, established in 1879, is the second oldest national park in the world. Inland, Cape Yorkrtee Valley draws birders to its grassy box and ironbark woodland.

  • Habitat: Heathland covers the sandstone ridges, dense forest clothes the slopes, and mangroves fringe the tidal flats where the Hawkesbury meets the sea. Royal National Park adds temperate rainforest, beaches and mudflats. West of the mountains the Capertee Valley holds open grassy box and ironbark woodland.
  • When: Autumn suits the box and ironbark woodland inland, when flowering eucalypts pull in nectar feeders and honeyeaters move north in flocks. Late winter and spring bring the sandstone heath into flower, and honeyeaters gather on it then.
  • Getting there: Most of the Sydney sites are reachable by public transport, and a 2WD car covers the rest. Sydney has a major international airport and sealed highways run north, south and west. Camping in Royal National Park is available at set sites and bush camping needs a booking.
  • Look for: Rockwarbler, Pilotbird, Beautiful Firetail, Chestnut-rumped Heathwren, Superb Lyrebird, Regent Honeyeater, Turquoise Parrot, Diamond Firetail, Spotted Quail-thrush, Glossy Black Cockatoo, Southern Emu-wren, Tawny-crowned Honeyeater, Green Catbird, Speckled Warbler
  • Stops:
    • : One of the best known birding areas in Australia, worked mostly from the wooded roadsides and creek lines rather than from reserves. Regent Honeyeater, Turquoise Parrot, Painted Buttonquail and Diamond Firetail are the valley's birds.
    • : Heathland on sandstone ridges, forest on the slopes and mangrove on the tidal flats, where the Hawkesbury River meets the sea north of Sydney. The heath tracks hold Chestnut-rumped Heathwren and a long list of honeyeaters, and West Head is fairly reliable for Glossy Black Cockatoo and Yellow-tailed Black Cockatoo.
    • : The second oldest national park in the world, with rainforest, woodland, heath, mudflat, mangrove and beach inside one boundary. Rockwarbler, Pilotbird, Beautiful Firetail and Chestnut-rumped Heathwren are the local specialities.
  • Also covers: Capertee Valley, Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, Royal National Park, Sydney basin
  • Also watch for: Eastern Grey Kangaroo, Common Wallaroo and Common Wombat all occur in the box and ironbark woodland of the Capertee Valley.

The Hunter and the Barringtons

an internationally important estuary below a rainforest plateau

The Hunter estuary is recognised as internationally important, with extensive saltmarsh, mangroves and tidal ponds across Ash Island, Hexham Swamp and the Kooragang wetlands. Ash Island is best known for regular records of Eastern Yellow Wagtail, a northern migrant with very few sightings in eastern Australia. Barrington Tops rises inland and holds rainforest birds along the spine of the Great Dividing Range.

  • Habitat: Saltmarsh, mangrove, shallow ponds and tidal flats fill the estuary at the river mouth. Inland the Barrington plateau carries temperate rainforest at higher elevation, with wet and dry sclerophyll forest below it and grassy woodland through the Hunter Valley.
  • When: Migratory shorebirds are in the estuary through summer. Eastern Yellow Wagtail records at Ash Island have clustered between February and March. National park campgrounds inland fill over the summer holidays, so book a site well in advance.
  • Getting there: Newcastle lies north of Sydney and the two are linked by sealed highway. A 2WD car reaches every estuary site, and the bridge to Ash Island is signposted from the main road north of the city. Barrington Tops is a couple of hours further inland.
  • Look for: Eastern Yellow Wagtail, Great Knot, Black-tailed Godwit, Australasian Bittern, Eastern Grass Owl, White-fronted Chat, Mangrove Gerygone, Rufous Scrubbird, Olive Whistler, Red-browed Treecreeper, Russet-tailed Thrush, Swift Parrot, Regent Honeyeater, Turquoise Parrot, Diamond Firetail
  • Stops:
    • : Part of the Hunter Estuary, with saltmarsh, mangrove and shallow tidal ponds. The swale and ponds carry egrets and duck, and Freckled Duck has been recorded among them.
    • : A spit under the Stockton Bridge and the most reliable place on the estuary for the coastal migratory shorebirds. Great Knot, Bar-tailed Godwit, Grey-tailed Tattler and Far Eastern Curlew stage on the beach in front of it, and the birds gather two to three hours after high tide.
    • : One of the largest temperate rainforests in Australia, on a plateau rising to 1,500 metres. It holds one of the four remaining populations of Rufous Scrubbird, and the Gloucester Tops section takes you from subtropical rainforest low down to the higher forest in a morning.
  • Also covers: Ash Island, Barrington Tops National Park, Hunter coast, Stockton Sandspit
  • Also watch for: Platypus works the Gloucester River at Barrington Tops, and Eastern Water Dragon sits on the banks along the same track.

The Illawarra and the Shoalhaven: Barren Grounds to Jervis Bay

plateau heath specialists and a shelf edge pelagic

The sandstone heath at Barren Grounds and on the Morton plateau holds Eastern Bristlebird and Ground Parrot, both difficult birds elsewhere in the state. Comerong Island gathers summer shorebirds at the mouth of the Shoalhaven. A pelagic boat runs out to the shelf east of Wollongong and has turned up albatrosses, petrels and the occasional major rarity.

  • Habitat: Wet sedge and heathland cover the plateaus above the escarpment, with rainforest and dry eucalypt forest in the gullies below. At the coast, sandspits and beaches face open ocean, and the continental shelf lies about twenty nautical miles offshore.
  • When: Spring and early summer bring migrants into the area. Shorebirds crowd the mouth of the Shoalhaven through summer. Numbers offshore shift month by month, and albatrosses are most likely through the cooler half of the year.
  • Getting there: Sealed roads climb from the coast to the plateau reserves and a 2WD car reaches them all. Walking tracks across the heath range from short loops to routes of several hours. The pelagic departs from Wollongong Harbour and advance booking is essential.
  • Look for: Eastern Bristlebird, Ground Parrot, Southern Emu-wren, Pilotbird, Beautiful Firetail, Chestnut-rumped Heathwren, Striated Fieldwren, Crescent Honeyeater, Rockwarbler, Providence Petrel, Hutton's Shearwater, Shy Albatross, Black-browed Albatross, Terek Sandpiper
  • Stops:
    • : A hanging swamp plateau sits high on the Illawarra Escarpment and heath covers it. Ground Parrot, Eastern Bristlebird, Southern Emu-wren and Beautiful Firetail all live here, and Pilotbird calls from the forest just inside the entrance.
    • : The falls sit in Morton National Park, and the East Rim and West Rim tracks run out along the escarpment from them. Superb Lyrebird, Gang-gang Cockatoo, Green Catbird and Pilotbird are along the rim, and Rockwarbler keeps to the rocky stream below.
    • : Six hundred and sixty hectares in the delta of the Shoalhaven River hold tidal mudflat, mangrove swamp and littoral forest. It is a strong site for migratory waders, and the three habitats add waterbirds and bush birds to the same walk.
    • : The Jervis Bay end of the coast, with a botanic garden and the Telegraph Creek nature trail as the two birding walks. Eastern Bristlebird is often seen on the roadside verges inside the park.
    • : The day boat runs from here out to the edge of the continental shelf, about twenty nautical miles east. Over 100 seabird species have been recorded on these trips, with albatrosses, petrels and shearwaters the usual return.
  • Also covers: Barren Grounds Nature Reserve, Booderee National Park, Comerong Island Nature Reserve, Fitzroy Falls, Jervis Bay, Wollongong pelagic
  • Also watch for: Long-nosed Potoroo and Pygmy Possum live in the Barren Grounds heath. The Wollongong pelagic turns up Australian Fur Seal, Common Dolphin, Humpback Whale and Sperm Whale on the run out to the shelf.

The Riverina and the central west

mallee birds at the eastern edge of their range

Round Hill and the adjoining Nombinnie protect isolated populations of Red-lored Whistler and Malleefowl, and together they are the mallee hotspot of New South Wales. Fivebough at Leeton and Lake Cargelligo hold water when the surrounding country dries out, and both give a chance of Australian Painted-snipe. South of Wagga Wagga, The Rock stands as a single rugged hill on a flat plain, ringed by grey box and white box woodland.

  • Habitat: Mallee woodland and spinifex cover the reserves north of Lake Cargelligo. Shallow marshy wetlands sit among the irrigation country around Leeton. Further south the country is open eucalypt woodland of grey box, white box, Blakely's red gum and scattered white cypress-pine.
  • When: Autumn and spring are the best seasons, with pleasant daytime temperatures and nights that stay mild. Summer is very hot and winter nights drop below zero. Painted-snipe appear when shallow marshy conditions persist.
  • Getting there: Highways through the region are sealed and a 2WD car reaches most sites. Roads inside the mallee reserves are dirt and can need a 4WD after rain. Nature reserves in New South Wales are often closed to the public, so confirm access before travelling. Bush camping is possible in the mallee and there are motels in the nearby towns.
  • Look for: Red-lored Whistler, Malleefowl, Shy Heathwren, Chestnut Quail-thrush, Southern Scrub Robin, Gilbert's Whistler, Black Honeyeater, Orange Chat, Crested Bellbird, Australian Painted-snipe, Freckled Duck, Australasian Bittern, Speckled Warbler, Diamond Firetail, Red-capped Robin
  • Stops:
    • : Mallee in the middle of New South Wales joins the much larger Nombinnie Nature Reserve. The two protect isolated populations of Red-lored Whistler and Malleefowl, and Shy Heathwren, Southern Scrub Robin and Chestnut Quail-thrush share the same scrub.
    • : Lake Cargelligo sits on the Lachlan River floodplain in the central west. The treatment works south of the township draw large numbers of waterbirds. Freckled Duck, Blue-billed Duck and three species of crake are among them.
    • : A Ramsar listed wetland of 400 hectares with five kilometres of trail, viewing mounds and two hides. Australasian Bittern, Brolga and Superb Parrot are the birds it is known for, and the crakes work the shallow edges.
    • : Three hundred and fifty hectares of bush around a single rugged hill that stands out from a flat plain. The walking is easy at the base, and Speckled Warbler, Red-capped Robin and Brown Treecreeper are close to the car park.
  • Also covers: Fivebough Swamp, Leeton, Griffith, Lake Cargelligo, Round Hill Nature Reserve, The Rock Nature Reserve, Wagga Wagga
  • Also watch for: Sand Goanna and Stumpy-tailed Lizard are the usual company on the sandy tracks through the Round Hill mallee, and snakes are about in the warmer months.

The far west and the corner country: Broken Hill to Birdsville

grasswrens and gibber birds along the outback tracks

The corner country carries the arid specialities: Eyrean Grasswren on the dunes, Grey Grasswren in the lignum and Gibberbird out on the stony plains. The Birdsville and Strzelecki Tracks run north through it, and Sturt National Park is often the hottest place in New South Wales. Birdwatchers have died out here through poor preparation, so this is country to plan carefully.

  • Habitat: Sandy deserts, stony gibber plains and rocky ranges give way to rolling downs, with lignum choked watercourses and channel country that floods after rain and then dries again.
  • When: Autumn and spring bring mild days and nights and are the seasons to travel. Keep to the cooler months on the tracks, because summer temperatures are extreme and water is short. Birdlife responds fast after significant rain, when the vegetation transforms.
  • Getting there: The Birdsville and Strzelecki Tracks are unsealed and a 4WD is needed, along with extensive planning. Fuel, food and water are far apart, so plan each leg and carry reserves. Some country needs a permit, and permission should be sought from traditional landholders. Take care on foot away from the vehicle, because the landscape is vast, the landmarks are few and it is easy to become disoriented.
  • Look for: Eyrean Grasswren, Grey Grasswren, Gibberbird, Cinnamon Quail-thrush, Flock Bronzewing, Ground Cuckooshrike, Letter-winged Kite, Banded Whiteface, Grey Falcon, Chirruping Wedgebill, Chestnut-crowned Babbler, Pink Cockatoo, Eastern Bluebonnet, Inland Dotterel, Yellow Chat
  • Stops:
    • : River red gum country south-east of Broken Hill takes in the Menindee Lakes, and the Darling River runs along its eastern boundary. Water brings waterbirds in a good year, and the woodland holds Eastern Bluebonnet, Pink Cockatoo and Chestnut-crowned Babbler.
    • : Three hundred and forty thousand hectares of mulga and gibber in the far north-west corner of the state, with flat-topped mesas rising above the plain. Grey Grasswren, Cinnamon Quail-thrush, Flock Bronzewing and Gibberbird are the corner country birds here.
    • : A lake east of Thargomindah that can be viewed from the road bridge or from a walk in to the lakeside. Up to 60 waterbird species have been recorded, and the samphire flats on the west side hold Orange Chat and White-winged Fairywren.
    • : A township on Cooper Creek where the Strzelecki Track comes up from the south. The waterholes along the creek hold waterbirds, and the gibber plains around the town are one of the regular places for Gibberbird, with Chestnut-crowned Babbler, Chirruping Wedgebill and Bourke's Parrot nearby.
    • : The one stop for fuel and supplies about halfway between Marree and Birdsville. The sandhills beside the track hold Eyrean Grasswren, and Banded Whiteface is in the same country.
  • Also covers: Broken Hill, Innamincka and the Strzelecki Track, Kinchega National Park, Lake Bindegolly National Park, Mungerannie, on the Birdsville Track, Sturt National Park, Thargomindah, Tibooburra
  • Also watch for: Yellow-footed Rock Wallaby holds on in the gorges in the north of Mutawintji.

Canberra and the high country

crakes on the lake edge and lyrebirds in the ranges

Kelly Swamp sits in the Jerrabomberra wetlands at the eastern end of Lake Burley Griffin, and two hides look out over its mudflats. It is among the more reliable places in the country for crakes and rails. West of the city Tidbinbilla and Namadgi climb through wet forest and tall eucalypt to subalpine snow gum. Gang-gang Cockatoo is a constant through the ranges.

  • Habitat: Pools, channels and reed fringed swamps sit at the eastern end of the city lake, with exposed mudflats when levels drop. The reserves west of the city hold wetlands, grasslands, wet forest and dry woodland, and they rise through tall eucalypt to subalpine snow gum woodland along the range tops.
  • When: Summer brings shorebirds to the exposed mudflats at Kelly Swamp. Bassian Thrush is mainly a winter bird in the dense gullies. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons for the high country, where winter nights fall below zero.
  • Getting there: Canberra has a major airport and is linked to Sydney and the coast by sealed highway. A 2WD car reaches every site. Walking trails in the reserves run from short loops of a kilometre or two to management trails of twelve kilometres or more along the range.
  • Look for: Gang-gang Cockatoo, Baillon's Crake, Spotless Crake, Australian Crake, Lewin's Rail, Superb Lyrebird, Pilotbird, Spotted Quail-thrush, Bassian Thrush, Blue-billed Duck, Southern Whiteface, Speckled Warbler, Red-browed Treecreeper, Olive Whistler
  • Stops:
    • : Pools, channels and streams at the eastern end of Lake Burley Griffin, in the middle of Canberra. Kelly Swamp is the centre of it, and two hides look over mudflats that hold Latham's Snipe, Australian Crake, Baillon's Crake and Spotless Crake.
    • : Wetland, grassland, wet forest and dry woodland between the Tidbinbilla and Gibraltar Ranges. The Mountain Creek trails give Superb Lyrebird, Gang-gang Cockatoo and Pilotbird, and the longer Camel Back Trail climbs into snow gum for Spotted Quail-thrush.
    • : The park runs south from the Tidbinbilla boundary into the high country. Spotted Quail-thrush is regular along the ridge roads and the Square Rock track, alongside Superb Lyrebird, Wonga Pigeon, Pilotbird and Red-browed Treecreeper.
  • Also covers: Canberra, Jerrabomberra Wetlands Nature Reserve, Namadgi National Park, Tidbinbilla Nature Reserve
  • Also watch for: Tidbinbilla runs recovery programs for Northern Corroboree Frog and Brush-tailed Rock Wallaby, both of which can be seen along the sanctuary loop.

Melbourne and Port Phillip: Werribee and the You Yangs

Australia's largest waterbird gathering, an hour from the city

The Western Treatment Plant covers 10,500 hectares of lagoons and saltmarsh on the north-western shore of Port Phillip Bay, and in summer it can hold 20,000 shorebirds and 200,000 waterbirds. Two hundred and seventy species have been recorded inside the fence, and a hundred in a day is achievable. The dry granite hills of the You Yangs sit close by and add the woodland birds the bay lacks.

  • Habitat: Settling ponds, borrow pits and intertidal sand flats spread across a working sewage treatment plant, with saltmarsh along the shore and short grazed paddocks inland. The You Yangs are granite outcrops carrying dry eucalypt woodland, and the creek line on their western side holds birds of the drier north.
  • When: Summer brings peak shorebird numbers and the best odds on a vagrant, and a rising tide pushes the flocks off the flats onto the inland ponds where they are easiest to scan. Eucalypt flowering in the You Yangs usually runs from April to September and draws lorikeets and honeyeaters to the trees near the entrance.
  • Getting there: The plant lies south-west of Melbourne off the freeway, and entry needs a permit and a safety induction. Permit holders receive a key for the locked gates and a detailed map. Kirk Point at the end of Beach Road sits outside the gates and is open to everyone, so visitors without a permit can still work the shoreline there. The You Yangs are a signed regional park on sealed road from either Melbourne or Geelong.
  • Look for: Blue-winged Parrot, Cape Barren Goose, Brolga, Freckled Duck, Banded Lapwing, Pink-eared Duck
  • Stops:
    • : The largest sewage treatment works in Australia lies on the north-western shore of Port Phillip Bay, and in summer its ponds hold up to 20,000 shorebirds and 200,000 waterbirds. Entry needs a permit and a gate key, and Lake Borrie is the pond to work for Freckled Duck and Blue-billed Duck.
    • : A low granite range in dry woodland between Melbourne and Geelong. Swift Parrot feeds here when the eucalypts flower, Tawny Frogmouth roosts in the larger trees and Painted Buttonquail works the woodland floor.
    • : Open grassy woodland and wetland north of Geelong, run as a breeding site for Brolga and Australian Bustard. Magpie Goose, Cape Barren Goose and Freckled Duck are resident on the water.
    • : A swamp, wetlands and remnant bush on the Yarra River inside suburban Melbourne. The list runs to 148 species, Powerful Owl roosts in the dense vegetation and Australian Painted-snipe has turned up on the swamp.
    • : Part native garden and part untouched heathy woodland and wetland south-east of Melbourne. Southern Emu-wren holds the heath, and Chestnut-rumped Heathwren, Bassian Thrush and Brush Bronzewing are on the list.
  • Also covers: Banyule Flats Reserve, Geelong, Melbourne, Royal Botanic Gardens Cranbourne, Serendip Sanctuary, Western Treatment Plant, Werribee, You Yangs Regional Park

The Victorian coast: Port Fairy, Phillip Island and Wilsons Promontory

Heathland skulkers, a million shearwaters and shelf-edge seabirding

Wilsons Promontory is the southern tip of mainland Australia, a granite headland of coastal heath, rainforest gullies and the southernmost mangroves in the world. Phillip Island holds an estimated million Short-tailed Shearwaters around Cape Woolamai and a nightly penguin landing. Day boats from Port Fairy reach the continental shelf and offer some of the best pelagic birding anywhere.

  • Habitat: Coastal heath and banksia woodland over granite at the Prom, with intertidal flats in Corner Inlet that carry up to 30,000 shorebirds. Phillip Island is pasture and dune above burrow colonies. Tarra-Bulga protects cool temperate rainforest and tree ferns in the Strzelecki Ranges. The pelagic ground is the shelf edge, 40 to 50 km out in the Southern Ocean.
  • When: Short-tailed Shearwaters occupy the colonies from late September to April and stream back to Cape Woolamai at sunset. Summer brings migratory shorebirds to Corner Inlet and Shallow Inlet. Albatross and petrel variety on the pelagics is highest in the cooler half of the year, when Grey-headed and Light-mantled Albatross become possible.
  • Getting there: Wilsons Promontory is a long drive south-east of Melbourne on sealed road, and the serviced campground at Tidal River fills over holidays, with a ballot allocating sites at Christmas and Easter. Phillip Island is reached by bridge. Tarra-Bulga is signed from the highway at Traralgon and from Yarram. The Port Fairy pelagics are day boats that must be booked well ahead, and places are limited.
  • Look for: Southern Emu-wren, Beautiful Firetail, Ground Parrot, Little Penguin, Shy Albatross, Buller's Albatross
  • Stops:
    • : Day boats run from this far south-western Victorian harbour out to the continental shelf, some 40 to 50 km offshore. More than 60 seabird species have been recorded, Shy Albatross and Black-browed Albatross among them, and rough weather cancels many trips.
    • : An island in Western Port joined to the mainland by a bridge, with tidal mudflats, bush and surf beaches. Observation Point at Rhyll overlooks the flats for Great Knot and Bar-tailed Godwit, and the island is one of the easiest places for Cape Barren Goose.
    • : The southernmost tip of the Australian mainland, with granite headlands, white beaches and dense coastal heath. Beautiful Firetail and Forest Raven live here, Hooded Plover runs the beaches and Ground Parrot is the hard prize.
    • : Cool temperate rainforest and tall wet forest in the Strzelecki Ranges of Gippsland. Pilotbird holds the gullies here and this is one of the easiest places for Superb Lyrebird, which calls most in winter.
  • Also covers: Phillip Island Nature Parks, Port Fairy pelagic, Tarra-Bulga National Park, Wilsons Promontory National Park
  • Also watch for: Eastern Grey Kangaroo, Common Wombat and Echidna are all easy on the regenerating flats at the Prom, and Koala occupies the taller eucalypts along the Lilly Pilly Gully walk.

The Victorian Mallee and the box-ironbark

Mallee specialities on spinifex sandplain, nectar in the ironbark

Wyperfeld, Hattah-Kulkyne and Little Desert protect vast mallee over spinifex in Victoria's dry north-west, with more than twenty parrot species between them. The box-ironbark belt to the east flowers in winter and spring and pulls in the state's rarest nectar feeders. Terrick Terrick holds the largest intact native grassland left in Victoria.

  • Habitat: Mallee woodland with spinifex clumps on sand ridges, native pine plains, black box and river red gum along lake beds that fill only in flood. The box-ironbark parks east of there are open forest of white box, yellow box and ironbark on gravel country. Terrick Terrick mixes white cypress-pine woodland with reserved native grassland paddocks.
  • When: Spring is the peak, with the mallee birds calling and the woodswallows and trillers in. Autumn suits the box-ironbark, and the ironbark flowering that draws Swift Parrot and Regent Honeyeater runs through winter and spring, though it fails in some years. Mallee summers regularly pass 40 degrees and make midday birding hard.
  • Getting there: Every park is reached on sealed road with graded tracks inside, and several of the best mallee tracks need four wheel drive after rain. Wyperfeld is entered from the north or the south, Hattah-Kulkyne from the highway east of its township, and Chiltern from the Hume corridor. Bush campgrounds serve the mallee parks and visitors carry their own water and cooking gear.
  • Look for: Mallee Emu-wren, Striated Grasswren, Malleefowl, Red-lored Whistler, Regent Honeyeater, Plains-wanderer
  • Stops:
    • : A large mallee reserve in north-western Victoria with pine plains, red gum and black box woodland and heath around lake beds that fill only in flood. More than 20 parrots occur, Pink Cockatoo and Regent Parrot among them, and it is the one reliable Victorian site for Redthroat.
    • : Mallee and river red gum stretching from the highway east to the Murray River. The Nowingi Track is the walk birders use for Mallee Emu-wren, Striated Grasswren and Chestnut Quail-thrush.
    • : Sandy country under banksia, sheoak and tea-tree heath, proclaimed to protect Malleefowl. Slender-billed Thornbill, Rufous Fieldwren and Purple-gaped Honeyeater are here, and spring brings both the wildflowers and the peak of bird activity.
    • : Box-ironbark forest scattered with huge granite boulders north-west of Bendigo. Gilbert's Whistler, Crested Bellbird, Hooded Robin and Southern Whiteface are the birds to look for, and Diamond Firetail feeds in the grass.
    • : One of the largest unspoilt grasslands left in Victoria, with granite outcrops and native pine woodland. The park is known for Plains-wanderer, and Hooded Robin, Diamond Firetail and White-winged Chough hold the woodland.
    • : Box-ironbark forest on the western slopes of north-east Victoria, with a set of dams that pull birds in. Regent Honeyeater and Turquoise Parrot are the reason birders come, Swift Parrot arrives in winter and Painted Honeyeater in spring and summer.
  • Also covers: Bendigo, Chiltern-Mount Pilot National Park, Hattah-Kulkyne National Park, Kooyoora State Park, Little Desert National Park, Mallee, Terrick Terrick National Park, Wimmera, Wyperfeld National Park
  • Also watch for: Kangaroos and Emu are abundant around the lakes at Hattah-Kulkyne, and Yellow-footed Antechinus forages along logs and fallen branches in daylight at Chiltern.

Far East Gippsland and the Croajingolong coast

Victoria's warm corner, where the east-coast birds run out

Croajingolong spans almost 100 km of near-pristine coast from Sydenham Inlet to the New South Wales border. It carries Victoria's last Eastern Bristlebird population and its most dependable Glossy Black Cockatoos, and summer brings east-coast migrants that reach no further south. Green Cape just over the border adds cliff-top seabirding above the same heath.

  • Habitat: Coastal heath backed by tall eucalypt forest, warm-temperate rainforest in the gullies, casuarina woodland on the ridges and tidal sand banks in Mallacoota Inlet. Cabbage Tree Creek Flora Reserve protects a stand of Victoria's only native palm.
  • When: Summer brings Black-faced Monarch, Scarlet Myzomela and White-throated Needletail, and several of them are present in that season alone. The heath birds and the black cockatoos are resident. Ground Parrot is usually flushed from knee-high heath, so walk it slowly and early.
  • Getting there: Mallacoota sits at the end of a sealed road off the Princes Highway and is the base for the eastern half of the park. Wingan Inlet, Thurra River and Tamboon Inlet are remote and several need four wheel drive. Howe Flat, the bristlebird site, is reached on four wheel drive tracks from the New South Wales side or by boat across Mallacoota Inlet. Green Cape is signed off Edrom Road south of Eden.
  • Look for: Eastern Bristlebird, Glossy Black Cockatoo, Topknot Pigeon, Ground Parrot, Sooty Owl, Scarlet Myzomela
  • Stops:
    • : A town on a tidal inlet at the far eastern tip of Victoria, with bush, heath and estuary all within walking distance. Captain Stevenson's Point looks over the sand spits for Eurasian Whimbrel and Far Eastern Curlew, and the heathland walk is where Ground Parrot is looked for.
    • : A quiet settlement where the bush comes down to the water on the upper arm of the Mallacoota inlet. Glossy Black Cockatoo feeds on casuarina cones from November to January, Brown Gerygone is resident and the local Grey Goshawks are the white morph.
    • : A headland of coastal heath and sea cliffs on the far south coast of New South Wales. Ground Parrot is the draw, Striated Fieldwren and Beautiful Firetail are common in the heath, and albatrosses pass below the clifftop.
    • : A pocket of warm temperate rainforest in far east Gippsland holding Australia's most southerly stand of native cabbage tree palm. A short loop walk runs through it and Eastern Whipbird calls from the undergrowth.
  • Also covers: Cabbage Tree Creek Flora Reserve, East Gippsland, Gipsy Point, Green Cape, Mallacoota, Orbost
  • Also watch for: Lace Monitor is common around the Shipwreck Creek campsite in the warmer months, and Eastern Water Dragon basks on the rocks at Genoa Falls.

South Australia: Gluepot, the Flinders and the arid north

The last Black-eared Miner stronghold and the grasswren ranges

Gluepot Reserve covers 51,300 hectares of old-growth mallee in the Riverland and holds the last large population of Black-eared Miner. The Flinders Ranges rise north of Adelaide and carry Short-tailed Grasswren on their spinifex slopes. Port Augusta stands where the gulf meets the arid interior and gathers chats, wedgebills and nomadic honeyeaters.

  • Habitat: Old-growth mallee with spinifex and a chenopod understorey at Gluepot, quartzite ranges with river red gum creek beds and spinifex slopes in the Flinders, and saltbush plain, red sand dunes and shallow saline wetlands around Port Augusta.
  • When: Spring is best across all three, and autumn runs a close second in the Flinders, with warm days and cool nights. Flinders summers get very hot and make birding difficult. Nomadic honeyeaters at Port Augusta follow the emu-bush flowering, so their timing depends on recent rain.
  • Getting there: Gluepot is reached on a long, well maintained dirt track north of the Murray that ordinary vehicles handle in dry weather, and visitors bring all their own water, food and fuel. Bush camping at three laid-out sites is the only accommodation on the reserve. Wilpena in the Flinders is on sealed road from Hawker and most other park roads take two wheel drive unless there has been heavy rain. The arid lands botanic garden north of Port Augusta has a series of defined walking loops.
  • Look for: Black-eared Miner, Red-lored Whistler, Scarlet-chested Parrot, Short-tailed Grasswren, Chirruping Wedgebill, Striated Grasswren
  • Stops:
    • : 50,000 hectares of mallee scrub and dry woodland north of Waikerie, bought and run by BirdLife Australia and reached on dirt road. Black-eared Miner, Red-lored Whistler, Striated Grasswren and Scarlet-chested Parrot are the headline birds and about 190 species are possible.
    • : Rugged outback ranges north of Adelaide, with spinifex slopes and dry creek beds lined with ancient river red gums. Short-tailed Grasswren is the bird birders come for and it is hard work, while Red-capped Robin and Wedge-tailed Eagle are straightforward.
    • : A garden of arid-zone plants at the head of Spencer Gulf, with hides looking onto the eremophila. It is the most reliable place in the country for Chirruping Wedgebill, and Redthroat, Southern Whiteface and Zebra Finch come in to drink.
  • Also covers: Flinders Ranges National Park, Gluepot Reserve, Port Augusta Arid Lands Botanic Garden, Riverland
  • Also watch for: Yellow-footed Rock Wallaby comes down to graze in the Flinders gorges in early morning and late afternoon, and Euro, Red Kangaroo and Western Grey Kangaroo are widespread on the surrounding plains.

The southern coast: Yorke Peninsula, Kangaroo Island and Bool Lagoon

Western Whipbird scrub and a Ramsar lagoon

Innes National Park on the tip of Yorke Peninsula was declared after Western Whipbird was rediscovered there in 1962, and the bird remains widespread in its coastal scrub. Kangaroo Island is the third largest island in Australia, with 267 species recorded and a long list of endemic subspecies. Bool Lagoon inland from the coast regularly holds more than 20,000 waterbirds.

  • Habitat: Clifftop coastal heath merging inland into mallee, salt lakes and grassland at Innes. Kangaroo Island keeps more than a third of its area under park, with drooping sheoak stands, heath, mallee and rocky coast. Bool Lagoon and the adjoining Hacks Lagoon form ten kilometres of freshwater lagoon with tea-tree stands and reed.
  • When: Western Whipbird sings in the two hours after sunrise and the hour before sunset, especially in the breeding season, so those are the windows to work the scrub. Waterbird numbers at Bool Lagoon peak in spring, and the site is at its best when large areas sit under ankle-deep water. Glossy Black Cockatoo is easiest at American River in autumn as birds prospect nest hollows.
  • Getting there: Innes is a long drive west of Adelaide on sealed road. Kangaroo Island is reached by vehicle ferry from the mainland or by air, and a car is needed once there. Bool Lagoon lies south of Naracoorte and has several boardwalks and walking trails, and it closes on total fire ban days.
  • Look for: Western Whipbird, Rock Parrot, Glossy Black Cockatoo, Purple-gaped Honeyeater, Magpie Goose, Australasian Bittern
  • Stops:
    • : Coastal heath covers the clifftops at the southern tip of Yorke Peninsula. Western Whipbird was rediscovered here in 1962 and the find made the park, and Malleefowl, Rock Parrot and Hooded Plover also occur.
    • : Australia's third largest island, at the mouth of Gulf St Vincent, with more than a third of it reserved and no foxes or rabbits. The island race of Western Whipbird is easy to find and a small sedentary population of Glossy Black Cockatoo works the casuarinas.
    • : A chain of freshwater lagoons in the south-east of South Australia is listed as a wetland of international importance, and boardwalks cross it. Magpie Goose was re-established here from Northern Territory eggs, and Black Swan and Australian Shelduck gather in thousands.
  • Also covers: Bool Lagoon Game Reserve, Innes National Park, Kangaroo Island, Naracoorte
  • Also watch for: Western Grey Kangaroo and Emu are widespread at Innes, Bottlenose Dolphin works the shallows all year, and Southern Right Whale passes the coast between May and September.

Southwest Western Australia: Cheynes Beach and the Stirlings

Three great skulkers in one stretch of coastal heath

Two Peoples Bay is where the Noisy Scrubbird was rediscovered in 1961 after being presumed extinct, and the same coastal heath carries Western Bristlebird and Western Whipbird. Cheynes Beach along the coast offers all three within walking distance of one small township. The Stirling Range and Fitzgerald River add mallee heath, wandoo woodland and one of the richest floras in Australia.

  • Habitat: Dense, long unburnt coastal heath and shrubland on the south coast, with mallee heath, wandoo and karri woodland inland. The Stirling Range has over 1500 plant species recorded, and Fitzgerald River covers 329,882 hectares as a UNESCO biosphere reserve and an Important Bird Area.
  • When: Autumn is an excellent time on the south coast. The three skulkers call most at dawn and dusk in any season, and walking the roads and fire trails at first light is the way to get onto them. Orchid flowering in the Stirling Range runs from September to November, and the heath flowering that brings in honeyeaters follows the same window.
  • Getting there: All four sites lie east of Albany and are reached on sealed road, with the last stretches into the reserves on gravel. Call playback is prohibited at Two Peoples Bay and visitors keep to the walking tracks, both to protect fragile heath and to limit the spread of dieback. Camping is available inside Fitzgerald River and the Stirling Range, and Two Peoples Bay is worked as a day visit from Albany or Cheynes Beach.
  • Look for: Noisy Scrubbird, Western Bristlebird, Western Whipbird, Red-eared Firetail, White-breasted Robin, Carnaby's Black Cockatoo
  • Stops:
    • : A small coastal settlement east of Albany is ringed by heath and by Waychinicup National Park. It is the best known place to try for Noisy Scrubbird, Western Bristlebird and Western Whipbird, and Red-eared Firetail and White-breasted Robin are around the settlement itself.
    • : Woodland and heath around the lower Waychinicup River and its estuary, east of Albany. The park sits inside an Important Bird Area for Noisy Scrubbird, Western Bristlebird and Carnaby's Black Cockatoo, and the critically endangered western ground parrot survives here.
    • : Heathland and shrubland on a bay east of Albany. Noisy Scrubbird was rediscovered here in 1961 after being presumed extinct, and Western Bristlebird and Western Whipbird hold the same heath.
    • : A very large coastal reserve of heathland, mallee and timbered gullies between Bremer Bay and Hopetoun, much of it wilderness reached only on foot. Western Whipbird is more common here than at the Albany sites, Western Bristlebird is regular, and the roads close after rain.
  • Also covers: Albany, Cheynes Beach, Fitzgerald River National Park, Stirling Range, Two Peoples Bay Nature Reserve, Waychinicup National Park
  • Also watch for: Honey Possum feeds at banksia flowers in these heaths and is occasionally out in daylight, Two Peoples Bay holds the last wild Gilbert's Potoroo, and Quokka, Western Ringtail Possum, Western Brush Wallaby and Quenda all occur around Cheynes Beach.

Perth, Rottnest and the mid-west coast

Island salt lakes and terns, then gorge country up the coast

Rottnest Island lies off Fremantle and is limestone and low scrub around large permanent salt lakes, with Rock Parrot along the shore and Bridled, Roseate and Fairy Tern offshore. Kalbarri National Park sits far up the coast where the Murchison River cuts gorges through sandplain, and it marks the northern limit of Blue-breasted Fairywren and Western Yellow Robin. Between them the coast produces wintering albatross and passing shearwaters.

  • Habitat: Limestone and sand under low scrubby vegetation with several large permanent salt lakes on Rottnest. Kalbarri holds river gorge, high sea cliff, acacia shrubland and vast sandplain heath, and the heath carries over a thousand wildflower species.
  • When: Wildflower flowering at Kalbarri runs from July to October and brings in Black, Pied and White-fronted Honeyeater. Wedge-tailed Shearwater is at Rottnest from September to April, and winter puts Indian Yellow-nosed Albatross, Southern Giant Petrel and Little Shearwater within scope range of the lighthouse. Rufous Fieldwren is best worked at dawn or dusk in low coastal heath.
  • Getting there: Rottnest is reached by passenger ferry from Perth and Fremantle, and most visitors hire a bicycle, since a full circuit of the island is a 22 km ride. Kalbarri National Park surrounds the township of the same name well north of Perth and is reached on sealed road, with the walking trails signed from the park roads.
  • Look for: Rock Parrot, Bridled Tern, Fairy Tern, Banded Stilt, Blue-breasted Fairywren, Rufous Fieldwren
  • Stops:
    • : A low island off Fremantle reached by ferry, with salt lakes, beaches and low scrub. Rock Parrot, Banded Stilt and Banded Lapwing are the resident targets, Osprey nests on the island, and the crossing itself can produce Brown Skua.
    • : Gorges cut through multicoloured rock by the Murchison River, with sea cliffs and sand plains carrying over 1000 wildflower species. Bush Stone-curlew, Crested Bellbird and Rufous Whistler are birds of the sand plain, and Pacific Gull works the coast.
  • Also covers: Kalbarri National Park, Perth, Rottnest Island
  • Also watch for: An estimated 10,000 Quokka live on Rottnest and shelter under the trees around the golf course and the settlement through the day.

Tasmania and Bass Strait

Thirteen endemics on a compact island, plus the shelf edge

Tasmania holds thirteen endemic bird species and all of them are reachable within a few days of Hobart. Bruny Island has recorded every one and offers the best access to Forty-spotted Pardalote. Melaleuca in the south-west is the last breeding site of the Orange-bellied Parrot, and pelagics from Eaglehawk Neck have logged about eighty seabird species.

  • Habitat: Wet eucalypt forest, cool temperate rainforest, dry white gum woodland and buttongrass moorland, with alpine vegetation above the treeline at Mount Field. Melaleuca is buttongrass plain and tea-tree scrub inside the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area. King Island is mostly farmland with small remnant blocks of native forest.
  • When: The thirteen endemics are present year round. Most birders come from late spring to early autumn when temperatures are pleasant, and winter is cold and wet with snow limiting mountain access. Orange-bellied Parrot arrives at Melaleuca in early October and departs in March and April. Little Penguin and Short-tailed Shearwater come ashore at the Bruny neck at last light from September to February.
  • Getting there: Hobart is the gateway and a two wheel drive car reaches almost every site. Bruny Island is reached by vehicle ferry and Mount Field on sealed road from Hobart. Melaleuca has no roads and is reached by chartered light aircraft, by sea through Port Davey, or on foot along the South Coast Track or the Port Davey Track, and visitors must be entirely self-sufficient. King Island is reached by air from Victoria and northern Tasmania. A park entry permit is required for the national parks.
  • Look for: Forty-spotted Pardalote, Scrubtit, Tasmanian Nativehen, Green Rosella, Orange-bellied Parrot, Shy Albatross
  • Stops:
    • : An island off south-east Tasmania is reached by ferry from Kettering, and it is farmed in the north and largely bush in the south. All twelve Tasmanian endemics occur, Forty-spotted Pardalote is straightforward here, and Swift Parrot arrives to breed in summer.
    • : Wet forest and mountain country a short drive from Hobart, and Tasmania's first reserved ground. Eleven of the twelve Tasmanian endemics occur, among them Tasmanian Nativehen, Green Rosella, Yellow Wattlebird, Black Currawong and Scrubtit.
    • : Boats run from this narrow isthmus on Tasmania's east coast into cold and often rough water. The trips produce seabirds that are hard to see off the mainland, among them Grey Petrel, Southern Fulmar and Broad-billed Prion.
    • : A remote clearing sits in the button-grass moorland of Tasmania's south-west. Light aircraft, a boat through Port Davey and a multi-day coastal walk are the three ways in. It is the last breeding site of Orange-bellied Parrot, and a hide near the airstrip looks onto them. Ground Parrot and Southern Emu-wren are in the surrounding heath.
    • : An island in Bass Strait about halfway between Tasmania and the mainland, which makes it a stopover for Orange-bellied Parrot on migration. The island holds its own races of Scrubtit, Black Currawong and Green Rosella.
  • Also covers: Bruny Island, Eaglehawk Neck pelagic, Hobart, King Island, Melaleuca, Mount Field National Park
  • Also watch for: Echidna, Platypus, Eastern Quoll, Eastern Barred Bandicoot, Rufous-bellied Pademelon, Common Brushtail Possum and Common Wombat are all regular around the Mount Field campground.

The Red Centre

Grasswrens and spinifex specialists in the MacDonnell gorges

The West MacDonnell Ranges west of Alice Springs hold Dusky Grasswren, Spinifexbird and Rufous-crowned Emu-wren in spinifex and quartzite gorge country. Uluru and Kata Tjuta add Sandhill Grasswren and Banded Whiteface on dune and stony country to the south-west. The waste stabilisation ponds just south of Alice Springs put waterfowl, crakes and chats in the middle of the desert.

  • Habitat: Quartzite ranges cut by gorges with permanent waterholes and river red gum creek beds, spinifex flats and mulga shrubland between them. Uluru sits on red sand dune country with sparse shrub cover, and the flat stony ground nearby suits Banded Whiteface. The Alice Springs ponds are a chain of shallow settling ponds south of the town.
  • When: Autumn and spring bring mild days and nights and are the most comfortable seasons. Summer heat makes inland birding hard and is best avoided. Desert birds track rainfall, so good seasons bring Budgerigar and Crimson Chat in large numbers and put nomadic honeyeaters onto flowering emu-bush.
  • Getting there: Alice Springs is the base and most sites are day trips on sealed road. Uluru is a long drive south-west and most visitors stay overnight near it, with flights also connecting the two. Ormiston Gorge has a sealed access road usable year round, and its best birding is a loop walk of three to four hours through the pound.
  • Look for: Dusky Grasswren, Rufous-crowned Emu-wren, Spinifexbird, Painted Finch, Spinifex Pigeon, Sandhill Grasswren, Banded Whiteface
  • Stops:
    • : A long chain of ranges runs west from Alice Springs, and gorges with permanent waterholes cut through it. Dusky Grasswren, Spinifex Pigeon and Painted Finch are on the rocky slopes, and Ormiston Gorge is the set piece for Western Bowerbird and Rufous-crowned Emu-wren.
    • : Treatment ponds just south of Alice Springs that hold open water in a dry landscape, with 185 species recorded. A permit and a key are needed to get in, and waterbirds and shorebirds are the reason to come.
    • : Two great rock landmarks rise from spinifex sandplain in the middle of the Red Centre, 440 km south-west of Alice Springs. Around 178 species have been reported. Striated Grasswren, Banded Whiteface and Chiming Wedgebill are among them, and Spotted Nightjar comes out after dark.
  • Also covers: Alice Springs sewage ponds, Tjoritja (West MacDonnell) National Park, Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park
  • Also watch for: Black-footed Rock Wallaby occupies the rocky slopes close to Alice Springs and Common Wallaroo is widespread through the ranges.

Lord Howe and Norfolk: the Tasman islands

Two Pacific islands with land endemics and breeding petrels

Lord Howe holds the flightless Lord Howe Woodhen and almost the entire world population of Providence Petrel, which breeds on the slopes of Mount Gower between April and November. Norfolk supports three endemic species and is the only place in Australia for the Norfolk Robin. Fourteen seabird species breed in the Lord Howe group, and Phillip Island off Norfolk is the sole Australian breeding site of White-necked Petrel.

  • Habitat: Lord Howe is a narrow island dominated by the basalt peaks of Mount Lidgbird and Mount Gower at its southern end and the Malabar cliffs in the north, with about three quarters under permanent park preserve and a coral lagoon along its western shore. Norfolk keeps its remaining native vegetation in a national park around Mount Bates, with pasture over roughly a third of the island and two small islands lying to the south.
  • When: Summer is the richer season on both islands, with breeding seabirds and migrant shorebirds present. Providence Petrel and Little Shearwater breed in winter, when the islands are quieter overall. April and October can produce both summer and winter species, though total seabird numbers are lower than at the height of either breeding season.
  • Getting there: Both islands are reached by scheduled flights from mainland Australia. Lord Howe caps visitor numbers, so accommodation is arranged well in advance, and the island is small enough that bicycles are the usual transport. Norfolk needs a hire car and has a good network of sealed roads. Phillip Island off Norfolk is visited only on an organised trek with an accredited local guide, and access depends on the weather and on a reasonable level of fitness.
  • Look for: Lord Howe Woodhen, Providence Petrel, Norfolk Parakeet, Norfolk Gerygone, Slender-billed White-eye, Red-tailed Tropicbird, Kermadec Petrel
  • Stops:
    • : A narrow volcanic island 600 km east of the mainland, nearly three quarters of it permanent park preserve and dominated by the peaks of Mount Lidgbird and Mount Gower. Fourteen seabirds breed in the group, almost the whole world population of Providence Petrel nests on Mount Gower between April and November, and the flightless Lord Howe Woodhen walks the settled ground.
    • : A small subtropical island in the Pacific, closer to New Caledonia and New Zealand than to the Australian mainland. Norfolk Gerygone, Slender-billed White-eye and Norfolk Parakeet live nowhere else, Norfolk Robin occurs nowhere else in Australia, and Black-winged Petrel and Sooty Tern breed.
  • Also covers: Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island
  • Also watch for: Green Turtle is tame and approachable in the shallows at Old Settlement Beach on Lord Howe through the summer. Norfolk has almost no native land mammals, and Phillip Island was cleared of rabbits and other introduced mammals so the petrels could come back.
