Christmas Island and the Indian Ocean territories

Five endemic birds and the red crab migration

Christmas Island and the Cocos Keeling group are Australia's Indian Ocean territories. Christmas Island lies in the north-east of that ocean, closer to Java than to mainland Australia, and 63 per cent of it is national park. Five bird species occur nowhere else, and Abbott's Booby and Christmas Frigatebird are two of them. Some 20,000 Red-footed Boobies breed here. Its position also delivers vagrants down from South-East Asia.

  • Habitat: A limestone plateau of tall rainforest rising steeply above a lower forested terrace, ringed by jagged sea cliffs with a few small and awkward beaches. The plateau is the summit of a submarine mountain that rises 4200 m from the sea bed, so truly pelagic seabirds forage within sight of the lookouts.
  • When: Daily maximum temperatures sit between 26 and 28 degrees all year and nights rarely drop below 22. Most of the 2110 mm annual rainfall falls from December to April, which is also when cyclones are possible. The endemics can be found at any time, and Australian birders favour November to April for the chance of vagrants. The red crab migration follows the first monsoon rains, usually from late November to mid December.
  • Getting there: Scheduled flights run from Perth and many of them call at the Cocos Islands, so the two can be combined in one trip. A hire car is essential and a small four wheel drive is recommended, because most roads away from the north-east corner are dirt and the steeper tracks need clearance in the wet season. Many roads close during the red crab migration to reduce crab mortality, which restricts access to large parts of the island.
  • Look for: Abbott's Booby, Christmas Frigatebird, Christmas Imperial Pigeon, Christmas Boobook, Christmas White-eye, White-tailed Tropicbird, Christmas Swiftlet
  • Stops:
    • : A rainforested island in the Indian Ocean south of Java, with more than 60 per cent of it national park. Five species breed nowhere else, Abbott's Booby, Christmas Frigatebird, Christmas Imperial Pigeon, Christmas Boobook and Christmas White-eye, and Margaret Knoll is the vantage point for soaring seabirds.
  • Also covers: Christmas Island
  • Also watch for: The annual Red Crab migration takes vast numbers of land crabs from the rainforest plateau to the shore to spawn, the endemic Christmas Island Fruit-bat rides the updrafts at Margaret Knoll in the afternoon, and Whale Shark appears offshore around the crab spawning.

Preparation

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time to go birding in Australia?

The country runs two calendars. The tropical north is at its best in the dry season from May to November, when the tracks are open and birds gather at shrinking water. The south peaks in spring from September to November, when the mallee and woodland birds are calling and the heath flowers bring honeyeaters in. A trip that takes in both should follow the season rather than the map.

How many bird species does Australia have?

Around 900 species sit on the national list, and close to half of them breed in Australia and nowhere else. Whole families belong to the continent alone, the lyrebirds, the scrubbirds and the emu among them, which is why the birding here feels unlike anywhere.

How long do you need for a first trip?

Two weeks covers one corner of the country properly. Three weeks links two, and the common pairing is the tropical north with the southeast. A first list of four hundred species is realistic in three weeks and asks for a great deal of driving. A shorter trip works best inside a single region.

Can you bird Australia without a car?

A handful of places work on foot and on public transport. Cairns, Sydney, Melbourne and Perth all put strong birding within reach of a bus or a train, and day tours run out of each of them. The rest of the country needs a vehicle, because the sites sit down unsealed roads with no service on them. Most visiting birders hire a car for the whole trip.

How big are the distances?

Australia is a continent and the driving matches. Darwin to Cairns is two long days on the road, and Perth to the south coast is a comfortable one. Sites inside a single region usually sit an hour or two apart, so the jumps between regions are the ones worth flying. Domestic flights link every capital and most large regional towns.

Where do you go for the endemics?

Four areas carry the most. The Wet Tropics behind Cairns holds a run of rainforest birds found nowhere else, the border ranges south of Brisbane hold Albert's Lyrebird and Rufous Scrubbird, the south coast of Western Australia holds the three skulkers of the heath, and the mallee of Victoria and South Australia holds the grasswrens and the mallee whistlers. Tasmania adds thirteen more that live on the island alone. The 25 regions.

What about the seabirds?

The southern waters rank with the best in the world for albatross and petrel. Day boats run offshore from ports in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and Western Australia, and the winter months bring the largest albatross numbers close to the shelf edge. The trips out of Sydney and Wollongong are the easiest to reach from a city. A Bass Strait crossing adds shearwater and prion from the deck.

Are Christmas Island and Norfolk worth adding?

Each is a separate flight and each adds birds found nowhere else. Christmas Island has five endemic species and takes vagrants down from South-East Asia through the wet months. Norfolk and Lord Howe hold their own endemics and sit within reach of the east coast. All of them suit a second or third visit, once the mainland regions are covered.

Do you need a guide?

Most of Australia is straightforward to bird alone with a field guide and a car. Two things repay a local: the skulkers of the southwest heath and the night birds, which people find through knowing the exact territories. A guide also saves days on Cape York and in the mallee, where a stretch of country can look identical for kilometres.

What should a first trip skip?

Cape York, the Mitchell Plateau and the corner country all reward the effort and all cost days of hard driving for a short list of birds. The Red Centre is a short flight and makes a fine second week. A first visit gets more from the Wet Tropics, the southeast and one southern region, and it can leave the remote grasswrens for a return.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Often yes, and it varies by site. A good deal of the birding here happens from roadsides, hides and lodge grounds rather than on long walks, and some reserves keep flat, surfaced trails. Ask a lodge or reserve directly about step free access, surfaces and seating before you book. The Birdability Map records those details for birding sites, and their Access Considerations guide lists the questions worth asking. Coverage is thin outside the United States, so read a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable.

Birding Community

Alongside the national bodies below, Australia has 40 local bird clubs across 8 regions. See every Australian club by region.

BirdLife Australia The national bird conservation body and BirdLife partner, with dozens of local branches across the country. Visit Birdata BirdLife Australia's national bird monitoring database, open to any volunteer submitting survey data. Visit Aussie Bird Count A week long national citizen science count each October, run by BirdLife Australia, open to anyone. Visit Australasian Wader Study Group Volunteer group coordinating shorebird counts, banding and research across Australia and the flyway. Visit Australian Bird Study Association A member society supporting bird banding and research, publishing the journal Corella. Visit BirdLife Australia Raptor Group Special interest group for the study, conservation and management of Australian birds of prey. Visit Australasian Seabird Group A joint BirdLife Australia and Birds New Zealand group for seabird research, surveys and beach patrols. Visit
